```{r}
# Import the Data File
library(readr)
library(fpp2)
library(TTR)
library(lubridate)
library(zoo)
library(dplyr)

Natural_Gas_Prices <- read_csv("natural_gas_prices_monthly.csv")
# View(Natural_Gas_Prices)

My_Data <- Natural_Gas_Prices
attributes(My_Data)

My_Data$Month <- as.yearmon(My_Data$Month,"%Y-%m")

start_year <- year(min(My_Data$Month))
start_month <- month(min(My_Data$Month))
end_year <- year(max(My_Data$Month))
end_month <- month(max(My_Data$Month))

s <- ts(My_Data$Price, start = c(start_year,start_month), frequency = 12)
attributes(s)
plot(s)

# Plot and Inference
plot(s,
     main = paste("Time Series Plot for Natural Gas Prices"),
     xlab = "Year",
     ylab = "Natural Gas Prices",
     col = "black",
     lwd = 2)

# The natural gas prices seem to spike every few years in a regular time interval. However, the intensity of the spikes vary throughout the years. Around 2001, a bigger spike is observed because this was the time when US experienced the most frigid winter in approximately 90 years, therefore there was an increased demand for heating which was not possible to be compensated by low production of natural gas leading up to 2001. Around 2005, there is a price spike after hurricanes Katrina and Rita. The natural disasters led to production disruptions, higher demand and supply shortages of natural gas. Last higher spike around 2009 was due to a combination of economic recession and financial instability. From a forecasting point of view, these historical spikes can skew our model's predictions, so the data will be truncated around November 2009 for better forecasting. 

series <- window(s, start = c(2009,11))
plot(series,
     main = paste("Time Series Plot for Natural Gas Prices"),
     xlab = "Year",
     ylab = "Natural Gas Prices",
     col = "black",
     lwd = 2)

acf(series, 
    main = paste("Autocorrelogram Plot for Natural Gas Prices"))

# The ACF trend shows that the plot declines at a faster pace eventually falling below the significant line. Based on the plot, there are no repeating spikes or regular cyclical patterns indicating no specific evidence of seasonality in this dataset. This can mean nearly stationary time series. For modeling purposes, it also suggest that the data follows a random walk model which will be explored in the later steps.

# Central Tendency
summary(series)

boxplot(series,
        main = "Boxplot For Natural Gas Prices",
        ylab = "Value")

# The median of the boxplot is 2.990, however since the median line is closer to the bottom of the box, it proves that the distribution is right (positive)-skewed. The IQR of this boxplot is 1.256, and the relative IQR is 0.42, which indicates moderate variability in the data set. There are only 2 outliers also suggesting that the majority of our data falls in the expected range.

# Decomposition
stl_decomp <- stl(series,s.window ="periodic")
stl_decomp
plot(stl_decomp)
attributes(stl_decomp)

# Yes the time series is seasonal because the seasonality plot spikes at regular 12 month interval in a cyclical pattern. However, the seasonal component has a smaller amplitude therefore it is weak relative to the level and trend of the series.

decomp_natural_gas_prices <- decompose(series)
decomp_natural_gas_prices

# The decomposition is additive.

monthly_indices <- decomp_natural_gas_prices$seasonal[1:12]
monthly_indices

# The monthly indices are: 0.062747299, 0.129913966, 0.124038966, -0.041627701, -0.133535108, -0.103396219,-0.055586034, 0.069663966, 0.055580633, -0.042336034, -0.003711034, -0.061752701.

# The monthly time series value for February is the highest (0.129913966) and May is the lowest   (-0.133535108). 

# The time series value for February is the highest because it is peak winter season therefore due to lower temperatures, the demand for natural gas increases due to high demand in heating. The time series value is lowest in May because it is the start of summer so it is not hot enough for the demand for cooling systems to increase, therefore the demand for natural gas is lower. 

seasadj <- seasadj(stl_decomp)
plot(seasadj)
lines(series, col="Red")

# Seasonality does not have big fluctuations in the values of the time series because it is stable so even without seasonality, the graph follows the original time series plot.

# ETS with Seasonality
ets_model <- ets(series) 
ets_model
plot(ets_model)

ets_forecast <- forecast(ets_model,h=12)
ets_forecast
plot(ets_forecast)

accuracy(ets_forecast)

attributes(ets_forecast)
ets_model$mse

# Performed the ETS model because seasonality was observed in the decomposition analysis, therefore wanted to run a model that did not require a strong autocorrelation to understand more. As observed this model has a MAPE of 8.742296 which is less than 10%, so this is a good indicator that the random forecast as expected is performing well. In the next year ahead, the natural gas prices will be $2.30.

# Naive Method
naive_model <- naive(series)
plot(naive_model)

naive_residuals <- residuals(naive_model)
naive_residuals

plot(naive_residuals,
     main = "Residuals from Naive Forecast for Natural Gas Prices",
     ylab = "Residuals", xlab = "Time",
     col = "blue", type = "l")
abline(h = 0, col = "red")

# Since the plot fluctuates around 0 the naive model seems to have no strong bias, it does not consistently overpredict or underpredict the data. However, there are certain months where the model's predictions were off potentially due to unexpected events, since the model takes the last value to forecast it can be said that it does not capture the short-term volatility in natural gas prices.

hist(naive_residuals,
     main = "Histogram of Residuals",
     xlab = "Residuals",
     col = "lightblue")

# The histogram roughly forms a bell-shaped curve centered around 0, however it is slightly higher left of the zero, indicating the histogram is slightly skewed to the right. The model occasionally underpredicts more strongly than it overpredicts. Since the histogram is not perfect bell-shaped, it means that the model probably fails to capture more seasonal/sudden variations. 

plot(as.numeric(fitted(naive_model)), residuals(naive_model),
     main = "Residuals vs Fitted Values",
     xlab = "Fitted Values",
     ylab = "Residuals",
     col = "steelblue", pch = 19)
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lwd = 2)

# The plot forms a scattered plot, where the values fitted at or below 4 are tightly clustered around 0 and the values fitted above 4 are spread out both negatively and positively. This basically indicates that the variance of residuals is not constant because there is small variance at lower fitted values and large variance at higher fitted values. There is also a remainder of some trend at the lower fitted values that the model does not capture.

plot(as.numeric(series), residuals(naive_model),
     main = "Residuals vs Actual Values",
     xlab = "Actual Values",
     ylab = "Residuals",
     col = "navy", pch = 19)
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lwd = 2)

# The plot forms a scattered plot, where the actual values at or below 4 are tightly clustered around 0 and the actual values above 4 are spread out both negatively and positively. This basically indicates that the variance of residuals is not constant because there is small variance at lower actual values and large variance at higher actual values.

Acf(naive_residuals)

# ACF plot has spikes between the significant line except for lag 3, this indicates that the residuals are uncorrelated, therefore the model is an adequate fit and it can be used for industry level decision-making.

accuracy(naive_model)

naive_forecast <- naive(series,12)
naive_forecast
plot(naive_forecast)

# The MAPE for this type of forecast is 8.706228 which is less than 10%, so this is a good indicator that the naive forecast is performing well.

# In 1 year, the time series value for the natural gas prices will be $2.30.

# The forecast is taking the last value and predicting the values for the next whole year for the point level forecast. However, in order to understand long-term capital planning, macroeconomy and formulate geopolitical strategy based on natural gas prices, high 80-95% range of $4.11 - $5.06 should be considered.

# Random Walk
rwf_model <- rwf(series,12)
rwf_model <- rwf(series, drift=TRUE)

rwf_residuals <- residuals(rwf_model)
rwf_residuals

plot(rwf_residuals,
     main = "Residuals from Random Walk Forecast for Natural Gas Prices",
     ylab = "Residuals", xlab = "Time",
     col = "blue", type = "l")
abline(h = 0, col = "red")

# The plot indicates that the model captured the main pattern of the model because there are random fluctuations around 0 except for the few years that had extremely high and low spikes, however these spikes did not have extremely high/low amplitudes. 

hist(rwf_residuals,
     main = "Histogram of Residuals",
     xlab = "Residuals",
     col = "lightblue")

# The histogram roughly forms a bell-shaped curve centered around 0, however it is slightly higher left of the zero, indicating the histogram is slightly skewed to the right. The model occasionally underpredicts more strongly than it overpredicts. Since the histogram is not perfect bell-shaped, it means that the model probably fails to capture more seasonal/sudden variations.

plot(as.numeric(fitted(rwf_model)), residuals(rwf_model),
     main = "Residuals vs Fitted Values",
     xlab = "Fitted Values",
     ylab = "Residuals",
     col = "steelblue", pch = 19)
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lwd = 2)

# The plot forms a scattered plot, where the values fitted at or below 5 are tightly clustered around 0 and the values fitted above 5 are spread out both negatively and positively. This basically indicates that the variance of residuals is not constant because there is small variance at lower fitted values and large variance at higher fitted values. There is also a remainder of some trend at the lower fitted values that the model does not capture.

plot(as.numeric(series), residuals(rwf_model),
     main = "Residuals vs Actual Values",
     xlab = "Actual Values",
     ylab = "Residuals",
     col = "navy", pch = 19)
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lwd = 2)

# The plot forms a scattered plot, where the actual values at or below 4.5 are tightly clustered around 0 and the actual values above 4.5 are spread out both negatively and positively. This basically indicates that the variance of residuals is not constant because there is small variance at lower actual values and large variance at higher actual values.

Acf(rwf_residuals)

# ACF plot has spikes between the significant line except for lag 3, this indicates that the residuals are uncorrelated, therefore the model is an adequate fit and it can be used for industry level decision-making.

accuracy(rwf_model)

rwf_forecast <- rwf(series,12)
rwf_forecast <- rwf(series, drift = TRUE)
rwf_forecast
plot(rwf_forecast)

# The MAPE for this type of forecast is 8.656243 which is less than 10%, so this is a good indicator that the random forecast as expected is performing well.

# In 1 year, the time series value for the natural gas prices will be $2.19.

# Simple Moving Averages
plot(series,
     main = paste("Time Series Plot for Natural Gas Prices"),
     xlab = "Year",
     ylab = "Natural Gas Prices",
     col = "black")

MA3_forecast <- ma(series,order=3)
lines(MA3_forecast, col = "red")

MA6_forecast <- ma(series,order=6)
lines(MA6_forecast, col = "blue")

MA9_forecast <- ma(series,order=9)
lines(MA9_forecast, col = "green")

# It is observed that the moving average of the order 3 is the best fit that is closest to the data set plot. So in forecasting the next 12 months, we will be using that fit.

# Moving Average with the Order = 3
MA3_model <- ma(series, order = 3, centre = FALSE)
MA3_f <- forecast(MA3_model, h = 12)
MA3_f
plot(MA3_f)

# Based on the moving average of order 3 forecast, the natural gas price in July 2021 will be $2.58.

accuracy(MA3_f)

MA6_model <- ma(series, order = 3, centre = FALSE)
MA6_f <- forecast(MA6_model, h = 12)
MA6_f
plot(MA6_f)

accuracy(MA6_f)

MA9_model <- ma(series, order = 3, centre = FALSE)
MA9_f <- forecast(MA9_model, h = 12)
MA9_f
plot(MA9_f)

accuracy(MA9_f)

# As the moving average order goes up, the forecasted line stays at the same smoothness and the MAPE value also remains the same. In this case, the series is dominated by noise and a trend can't be extracted in this model. The best forecast is close to naive forecast, therefore every Moving Average order becomes equivalent.

# Simple Smoothing
ses_model <- ses(series,12)
plot(ses_model)
summary(ses_model)

# The value of alpha is 0.9999. Since the alpha is almost equal to 1 so the model places all of the weight on the most recent observation and it is likely very volatile. The time series as observed earlier through other models is identical to Naive forecast.

# The initial state value is 3.66.

# The value of sigma is 0.4082. Since sigma is closer to 0, the forecast has smaller errors and it can be accepted that the model fits the data well. There is going to be high variability and randomness around predicted values making them less accurate.

ses_residuals <- residuals(ses_model)
ses_residuals

plot(ses_residuals,
     main = "Residuals from SES Forecast for Natural Gas Prices",
     ylab = "Residuals", xlab = "Time",
     col = "blue", type = "l")
abline(h = 0, col = "red")

# The plot indicates that the model captured the main pattern of the model because there are random fluctuations around 0 except for the few years that had extremely high and low spikes, however these spikes did not have extremely high/low amplitudes. 

hist(ses_residuals,
     main = "Histogram of Residuals",
     xlab = "Residuals",
     col = "seagreen")

# The histogram roughly forms a bell-shaped curve centered around 0, however it is slightly higher left of the zero, indicating the histogram is slightly skewed to the right. The model occasionally underpredicts more strongly than it overpredicts. Since the histogram is not perfect bell-shaped, it means that the model probably fails to capture more seasonal/sudden variations.

plot(as.numeric(fitted(ses_model)), residuals(ses_model),
     main = "Residuals vs Fitted Values",
     xlab = "Fitted Values",
     ylab = "Residuals",
     col = "steelblue", pch = 19)
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lwd = 2)

# The plot forms a scattered plot, where the values fitted at or below 5 are tightly clustered around 0 and the values fitted above 5 are spread out both negatively and positively. This basically indicates that the variance of residuals is not constant because there is small variance at lower fitted values and large variance at higher fitted values. There is also a remainder of some trend at the lower fitted values that the model does not capture. 

plot(as.numeric(series), residuals(ses_model),
     main = "Residuals vs Actual Values",
     xlab = "Actual Values",
     ylab = "Residuals",
     col = "navy", pch = 19)
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lwd = 2)

# The plot forms a scattered plot, where the actual values at or below 4.75 are tightly clustered around 0 and the actual values above 4.75 are spread out both negatively and positively. This basically indicates that the variance of residuals is not constant because there is small variance at lower actual values and large variance at higher actual values. 

Acf(ses_residuals)

# ACF plot has spikes between the significant line except for lag 3, this indicates that the residuals are uncorrelated, therefore the model is an adequate fit and it can be used for industry level decision-making.

accuracy(ses_model)

ses_forecast <- ses(series,12)
ses_forecast
plot(ses_forecast)

# The MAPE for this type of forecast is 8.639378 which is less than 10%, so this is a good indicator that the simple exponential smoothing forecast is performing well.

# In 1 year, the time series value for the natural gas prices in August 2021 will be $2.29.

# Holt-Winters
HW_model <- HoltWinters(series)
plot(HW_model)

HW_model$alpha

# The alpha = 0.7302479, therefore the level updates very quickly and the dataset is highly volatile to recent changes in values.

HW_model$beta

# Beta for this dataset are equal to 0. The beta component being equal to 0 means that there is no meaningful trend extracted by this model. The trend does not change over time and stays constant. 

HW_model$gamma

# The gamma component being equal to 0.9763966 means that the dataset updates the seasonal component aggressively each period. The seasonality is varying year to year.

HW_model$coef
# a = 1.95347964 is the initial level of the series at the start. This is the baseline around which the series oscillates. 

# b = -0.02968240 is the initial trend. There is a slight negative trend at the start and the series decreases very slowly.

# s1 - s12 values are the seasonal indices for months 1 to 12. These values basically represent the monthly effect of each month relative to the level indicated by a. Positive values are above baseline and negative values are below baseline.

HW_residuals <- residuals(HW_model)
HW_residuals

sigma <- sd(HW_residuals, na.rm = TRUE) 
sigma

# Sigma = 0.440554; Based on the sigma value, the model deviates by about 0.440554 units, which means that the model relative error is 22.6%. Since the forecasting model relative error is above 10%, the model is not accurate and most forecasts are within +/- 22.6% of the actual values. This leads to a standard deviation which is not acceptable based on this sigma.

plot(HW_residuals,
     main = "Residuals from Holt-Winters Forecast for Natural Gas Prices",
     ylab = "Residuals", xlab = "Time",
     col = "blue", type = "l")
abline(h = 0, col = "red")

# The plot indicates that the model captured the overall pattern of the dataset because there are random fluctuations around 0 however there are constant high and low spikes throughout the years. 

hist(HW_residuals,
     main = "Histogram of Residuals",
     xlab = "Residuals",
     col = "lightblue")

# The histogram roughly forms a bell-shaped curve centered around 0, however it is slightly higher left of the zero, indicating the histogram is slightly skewed to the right.

plot(fitted(HW_model), residuals(HW_model),
     main = "Residuals vs Fitted Values",
     xlab = "Fitted Values",
     ylab = "Residuals",
     col = "steelblue", pch = 19)
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lwd = 2)

# The xhat plot follows the shape of the actual data very closely, therefore it can be interpreted that the model captures the overall pattern well. The level section mirrors the xhat plot but it is smoother and decreases gradually over time. It can be noted that the natural gas prices dropped in the later periods. The trend line is flat meaning the model does not have a strong upward or downward growth, therefore it stays constant. The seasonality oscillates between -0.6 and 0.4. The pattern is not consistent indicating that the seasonality is volatile, shifting/varying year to year.

plot(as.numeric(tail(series, length(residuals(HW_model)))), residuals(HW_model),
     main = "Residuals vs Actual Values",
     xlab = "Actual Values",
     ylab = "Residuals",
     col = "navy", pch = 19)
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lwd = 2)

# The plot forms a scattered plot, where the actual values at or below 4.75 are tightly clustered around 0 and the actual values above 4.75 are spread out both negatively and positively. This basically indicates that the variance of residuals is not constant because there is small variance at lower fitted values and large variance at higher fitted values.

Acf(HW_residuals)

# ACF plot has all of the spikes between the significant line. Overall, the graph indicates that the residuals are uncorrelated and so the model is an adequate fit.

HW_forecast <- forecast(HW_model,12)
HW_forecast
accuracy(HW_forecast)
plot(HW_forecast)

# The MAPE for this type of forecast is 10.46277 which is around 10%, so this is a good indicator that the Holt Winters forecast is still performing good. The model captures overall trend and level reasonably well and it has an acceptable level of accuracy.

# In 1 year, the time series value for the natural gas prices in August 2021 will be $1.94.

# The forecast is mimicking the original plot, so it is adding some noise back into the forecast, therefore the forecast takes the trend of the overall plot of the actual dataset, then it looks into the next year's forecast. 

# ARIMA
arima_model <- auto.arima(series, trace=TRUE, stepwise = FALSE)
arima_model
attributes(arima_model)

# The output by the ARIMA model is (2,1,2). The auto regression portion indicates that the model takes 2 lags to model the past momentum. Since the natural price time series is almost stationary because there is no seasonality observed in the initial ACF plot, therefore the ARIMA model applied a first difference. The Moving Average portion is equal to 2 which is trying to correct the errors intensely. In this case, the AR and MA portion almost cancel each other out, this further proves a smooth, trending pattern with no strong seasonal structure. The data is behaving like a random walk with some short-term corrections, however there is not enough randomness for the complex ARIMA model to be stable. ARIMA (2,1,2) is trying to fit patterns that are not really there so it is either overfitting or there is weak signal and high noise in the data, which is inline with the expectation of the natural gas prices.

# Sigma^2 = 0.1511, the errors in this case are relatively small, after the ARIMA model was applied, the remaining noise has low variance and the model fits data closely, however due to unstable coefficients this model will not provide good forecasting.

# AIC = 130.15 and BIC = 144.45, which is extremely higher, BIC punishes the complexity where the ARIMA overfits the noise, therefore the data does not support such a complex model. Similar to earlier observations, a simpler model fits better in terms of this dataset.

Acf(arima_model$residuals) 

# The ACF of residuals is within the significant line so the model captures all the patterns available in the dataset. The residuals behave like white noise. Although the model is statistically appropriate, it still does not mean it is fitting for the dataset and good for forecasting.

Box.test(residuals(arima_model), lag=20, type="Ljung")

# The p value for Box-Ljung test is 0.9288. This means that ARIMA model explains all the autocorrelation in the data. The residuals are random AKA white noise. The model is statistically valid with no remaining patterns left to be modeled, however the overfitting makes it a less optimal choice for industrial decision-making related to macroeconomic and geopolitical strategies based on natural gas prices.

plot.ts(residuals(arima_model), 
        main = "Residuals from ARIMA Model for Natural Gas Prices",
        ylab = "Residuals", 
        xlab = "Time",
        col = "blue", type = "l")
abline(h = 0, col = "red")

# Since the plot fluctuates around 0 the naive model seems to have no strong bias, it does not consistently overpredicts or underpredicts the data. However, there are certain months where the model's predictions were off potentially due to unexpected events, the model almost overfits nonexistenting patterns in the dataset.

hist(arima_model$residuals)

# The histogram roughly forms a bell-shaped curve centered around 0, however it is slightly higher left of the zero, indicating the histogram is slightly skewed to the right.

tsdiag(arima_model)

# Most standardized residuals falls between +/- 2 with a few spikes. There is no clear trend, no long swings or clustering of errors. Residuals behave like random noise, there is no leftover trend or seasonality. The model is not systemically under- or over-predicting.

# All lags except for lag 0 is inside the significant lines. There is no autocorrelation left and ARIMA model captured all the structure in the data. The ARIMA model is statistically correct and not missing anything.

# Based on the p values for Ljung-Box satistic plot, the model does not leave behind systematic structure. The model's residuals behave exactly like white noise and it not mis-specified.

arima_forecast <- forecast(arima_model,h=5,level=c(99.5))
arima_forecast

# Based on the ARIMA model, the next 5 period forecast indicates that the natural gas price by January 2021 is expected to be $2.29.

accuracy(arima_forecast)

# The MAPE for this type of forecast is 8.633081 which is less than 10%, so this is a good indicator that the ARIMA forecast is performing well. However, as mentioned earlier the model is overfitting the data and although it is not missing any patterns to model, it is not optimal to use this model for this dataset.

plot(arima_forecast)

# Accuracy
Naive <- accuracy(naive_model)
RandomWalk <- accuracy(rwf_model)
ETS <- accuracy(ets_forecast)
MA3 <- accuracy(MA3_f)
MA6 <- accuracy(MA6_f)
MA9 <- accuracy(MA9_f)
SES <- accuracy(ses_model)
HoltWinters <- accuracy(HW_forecast)
Arima <- accuracy(arima_forecast)

models <- list(
  Naive = Naive,
  Random_Walk = RandomWalk,
  ETS = ETS,
  MA3 = MA3,
  MA6 = MA6,
  MA9 = MA9,
  SES = SES,
  HoltWinters = HoltWinters,
  ARIMA = Arima
)

accuracy_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(models), function(name) {
  acc <- models[[name]][1, c("ME", "RMSE", "MAE", "MPE", "MAPE", "MASE", "ACF1")]
  df <- data.frame(
    Model = name,
    ME = acc["ME"],
    RMSE = acc["RMSE"],
    MAE  = acc["MAE"],
    MPE = acc["MPE"],
    MAPE = acc["MAPE"],
    MASE = acc["MASE"],
    ACF1 = acc["ACF1"],
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  rownames(df) <- NULL
  return(df)
}))

rownames(accuracy_table) <- NULL
accuracy_table

# Based on the accuracy measures all the models have a MAPE that is less than or around 10%, which means that all the models are an accurate fit to the dataset. In this case, we have the ability to pick the model that best fits our business needs. Although Moving Average models have better MAPE, the models behave like a Naive model. Additionally, all the other models converge to behave like Naive forecast model. Therefore, considering cost efficiency, ease of understanding, faster computation, reduced overfitting risk, and easier maintenance, Naive model would be the recommendation to be used in case of predicting Natural Gas prices. Holt Winters model for this dataset is the worst model comparatively because this model has unstable seasonality so it varies year to year.

# Conclusion
# Trend: This dataset has a relatively stable trend with no variability.

# Seasonality: it is unstable, peaking in February due to the high demands, and lower in May. Overall the seasonality is weak due to smaller amplitude high/low spikes and variable across the years.

# Distribution & Skewness: series is right-skewed, and variability increases from year to year. 

# Autocorrelation: residuals are uncorrelated indicating adequate model fit for all of the models.

# Based on the analysis and forecast, the Naive Model suggests that the forecasted value for natural gas prices in 12 months will be $2.30. In the next 2 years, the trend is expected to be decreasing and stable and seasonality is expected to be variable.

# Model Ranking for this dataset:
# 1. Naive: works well beyond the benchmarking model because the series is pretty stable.
# 2. Random Walk, Simple Exponential Smoothing (SES), ARIMA: good fit, reacts quickly to recent changes; in case of SES the high alpha proves that observation
# 4. Moving Average of any order: it has lower error but it converges to a Naive model so it is not an optimal choice
# 5. Holt-Winters: worst for this dataset, because seasonality is unstable in this model  
```
